clue.text: Novel objective of a Home Secretary

parts.note: Michael Howard was Britain's Home Secretary from 1993 to 1997; 'of' supplies his possessive
an objective is an aim or goal, an end

explanation.surface: A question about what a government minister is really aiming at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new, but it is the definition: E. M. Forster's novel. 'objective of a Home Secretary' is read as Howard's end, the Home Secretary being Michael Howard.
explanation.definitionFit: Howards End is a 1910 book by E. M. Forster, a work of fiction.

clue.text: Housework, note, is just a game

parts.note: HO is the usual abbreviation for house
OP, short for opus, is a musical or literary work
LA is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses domestic chores as mere play.
explanation.walkthrough: One word supplies two pieces here, and the commas around 'note' make it look like an aside rather than wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoopla is a fairground pastime where rings are tossed over prizes.

clue.text: Fancy getting my wish accommodated!

indicators.note: accommodated in the sense of adapted or adjusted, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: An excited exclamation at having a wish granted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accommodated' rearranges MY WISH into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A whim or caprice is a passing fancy, a playful notion.

clue.text: Severely warned — against unlawful assembly

parts.note: an idiom for giving a stern reprimand, which literally names the act of a magistrate proclaiming an old statute that ordered riotous crowds to disperse

explanation.walkthrough: The Riot Act (1714) was a British law; a magistrate read it aloud to order an unlawful crowd to break up, hence the idiom for a stern telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver a stern reprimand is the idiomatic sense, from reading the 1714 statute to disperse rioters.

clue.text: Italian girl finds organ is in disrepair

indicators.note: something in disrepair is broken and out of order, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that the church organ is falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disrepair' shuffles ORGAN IS IN; the 'in' is fodder as well as sounding like part of the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Signorina is the Italian title for an unmarried young woman, like Miss.

clue.text: Remarked on the absence of haymakers?

parts.note: an absence of something means there is no such thing
to ted is to spread out mown grass to dry, the work of haymakers

explanation.surface: Someone comments that the hay workers have not turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'absence of haymakers' as NO TED: ted is a farming verb for turning and spreading hay.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted can mean observed aloud or commented upon.

clue.text: Friend left in funereal mantle

parts.note: a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A friend has been left wearing mourning dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A pall is the cloth spread over a coffin, a covering at funerals.

clue.text: A crooner confronts fellow in Oxfordshire

indicators.note: confronts means faces, so the crooner stands right before the fellow in the answer

parts.note: Bing Crosby was the famous American crooner
a don is a college fellow, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A singer squares up to a university fellow somewhere in Oxfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is a fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college, apt for an Oxfordshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: Abingdon is a market town found south of Oxford, in that county.

clue.text: Member with a liking for pedantic barman

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
list is an old word for desire or inclination

explanation.surface: A club member is fond of a fussy bartender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barman' is not a bartender but a member of the legal Bar, a barrister; list (to wish) is archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: A legalist is someone strictly adhering to the letter of the law, like a pedantic lawyer.

clue.text: Being shoved aside while visiting Chinese monument

explanation.surface: A tourist at the Great Wall gets jostled out of the way.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means being ruined or pushed out; literally it describes a trip to the Great Wall in China.

clue.text: A board gaining Franco-German agreement

parts.note: oui is French for yes
ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: A company board wins approval from France and Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The board's name famously combines the French and German words for yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ouija is a lettered board used in seances to spell out messages.

clue.text: Become emotional when told to start work

explanation.surface: Someone told to begin their job gets upset.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving means emotionally stirring, so 'get moving' can be read as becoming emotional; normally it is an order to get going.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an order to hurry up; moving also means touching the feelings.

clue.text: Leslie returns to house in Africa

parts.note: Les is the short form of the name Leslie

indicators.note: returns means the little word to is written backwards

explanation.surface: A man called Leslie comes back to his home somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns TO into OT.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a kingdom in southern Africa, enclosed by South Africa.

clue.text: Cheated by convict going back to Irish county

parts.note: to be done is slang for being swindled

indicators.note: going back means the word for a convict is reversed

parts.note: a lag is slang for a convict

explanation.surface: Someone swindled by a prisoner returns to Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going back' turns LAG into GAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Donegal is a county in the far north-west of Ireland.

clue.text: Sign said note, spelling out names

indicators.note: spelling out suggests forming a word from letters set in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A notice spells out a list of names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spelling out' rearranges SIGN SAID NOTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Designations are titles or labels given to things.

clue.text: Fiddlers are away and free of obligation

parts.note: when players are away there are none, no
violinists form the strings section of an orchestra

explanation.surface: The violinists are absent, leaving the orchestra free.
explanation.walkthrough: With the fiddlers away there are no strings, an idiom for having no conditions attached.
explanation.definitionFit: An offer with no strings attached carries no conditions.

clue.text: Getting tired of laying paving stones

explanation.surface: A workman grows weary of putting down a path.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagging means tiring or weakening; it is also paving with flagstones.

clue.text: Egghead made a wisecrack when fitted out

parts.note: the head of egg is its first letter, E
to quip is to make a witty remark

explanation.surface: An intellectual made a joke when supplied with kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egghead' looks like an intellectual but gives the head of 'egg', E.
explanation.definitionFit: Equipped means supplied with the necessary gear.

clue.text: Cash in the hands of water companies

definitions.text: in the hands of water companies

explanation.surface: Money is being held by the utilities.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquid assets are holdings readily turned into money; a water company literally holds liquid.

clue.text: Sending cable to illegal Mayfair syndicate

parts.note: Mayfair is in London's W1 postal district, the 1 read as the letter I
a ring is a gang or syndicate, often a criminal one

explanation.surface: A telegram goes to a crime gang operating in an upmarket London area.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayfair is a wealthy London district with postcode W1; 'illegal' merely colours the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiring is an old term for telegraphing a message.

clue.text: In Armagh a statesman is appalled

indicators.note: In says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A politician in Armagh, Northern Ireland, is horrified.
explanation.walkthrough: Armagh is a county and city of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means struck with horror or shock.

clue.text: Ground protected against frost

explanation.surface: Soil is covered to keep it from freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' is not soil but the past tense of grind, as teeth are.
explanation.definitionFit: Gritted teeth are clenched and ground; roads are spread with grit before icy weather.

clue.text: Uniform material for military exercises

explanation.surface: Fabric for army kit used during manoeuvres.
explanation.definitionFit: Drill is a stout twilled cotton cloth; it is also parade-ground training.

clue.text: Doing a Scottish dance whilst tipsy

explanation.surface: Someone performs a highland jig while drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A reel is a lively Scottish dance; reeling also means staggering from drink.

clue.text: Devilish behaviour creates indelible impression

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
action is conduct or behaviour

explanation.surface: Mischievous conduct leaves a lasting mark.
explanation.walkthrough: IMP is a noun here though 'Devilish' is an adjective: the pair read as devilish behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Impaction is the state of being firmly packed or wedged in, a lasting compression.

clue.text: She can go back into motoring club

indicators.note: into means the reversed can goes inside the club's letters

parts.note: the AA is Britain's Automobile Association

indicators.note: go back means the word for can is written backwards

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A woman is able to rejoin the motoring club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go back' turns TIN into NIT, which goes 'into' AA. The AA is Britain's main breakdown-recovery motoring organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita is a woman's name, so it can stand for a female pronoun.

clue.text: Some fascinating ideas presented by French novelist

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Intriguing thoughts put forward by a writer from France.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'presented by'; that is the link joining the hidden run to the definition, which is just 'French novelist'.
explanation.definitionFit: André Gide was a Nobel-winning writer from France, author of The Immoralist.

clue.text: Ostentatious lamp used by a paparazzo

parts.note: flash means showy or ostentatious
a lamp is a light

explanation.surface: A showy light is carried by a celebrity photographer.
explanation.walkthrough: A paparazzo is a press photographer chasing celebrities, who would use a flash for pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographers use a flash, a brief bright burst, for pictures.
